headline: Old Harbor Drowns Again: Sea Wall Sector 7 Collapses, Hundreds Displaced
body:
Sector 7 of the Old Harbor temporary sea wall gave way at approximately 2:40 this morning, sending an estimated nine million liters of lake water through the Cormorant Street corridor and into the already-flooded ruins that roughly 3,000 squatters, Bore Rats, and unregistered residents call home. Emergency response teams from Ferrogate Transit—whose infrastructure contracts technically make them responsible for the barrier—arrived four hours after the initial breach, by which point the water had reached the second-floor mark on the old Chandler Warehouse complex. 'Four hours,' said Mireille Achebe-Santos, who pulled her two children onto a roof on Barge Row and waited out the surge. 'Four hours and not one siren.'

The Sector 7 panel had been flagged in three separate Ferrogate internal inspection reports dating back to 2150, all of which cited advanced polymer fatigue in the modular barrier joints. A source inside Ferrogate Transit's Infrastructure Division, speaking anonymously, confirmed to the Gray Zone Voice that repair contracts were deprioritized after the company redirected maintenance budgets toward the new Spires-to-Circuit elevated transit corridor. Ferrogate's public affairs office released a statement attributing the collapse to 'unprecedented hydrological pressure events' and promised a full review, a phrase they have used verbatim following each of the four previous Sector failures since 2141.

Casualty counts remain difficult to establish. Old Harbor's population is, by definition, undocumented—residents there have no corponation affiliation, no Quanta accounts, and no NovaMind registration that would flag them as missing to the city's emergency grid. Community volunteers from The Collective have been working the ruins since dawn, and their field coordinator, Dayo Mensah-Ostrowski, estimates at least forty people remain unaccounted for as of this broadcast. Ironclad security drones deployed to the perimeter officially to 'prevent looting' have been blocking Collective aid boats from entering the deepest affected zones.

This is the fifth major Old Harbor flood event in eleven years. The Federal Remnant's Great Lakes Authority has repeatedly cited jurisdiction ambiguities between Ferrogate Transit and Palladian Holdings over the sea wall maintenance contracts as the reason no permanent repairs have been funded. Residents say they have stopped waiting for an explanation.
aftermath: The Lake Monitor's subsequent investigation confirmed the three suppressed inspection reports, triggering a public inquiry that Ferrogate Transit's legal division successfully delayed for two years through procedural filings.
runner_relevance: The flood generated overlapping runner contract types within hours. Search-and-extraction work pulled unregistered residents and stranded Bore Rat operators out of the surge zone for flat fees paid in cash quanta by Collective organizers. Simultaneously, Ferrogate Transit quietly hired runners to locate and retrieve the three internal inspection reports from the desks of engineers who'd gone public-facing—data retrieval and document suppression contracts that paid 15,000–20,000 quanta but required extreme discretion. Ironclad's perimeter deployment created a secondary sabotage market: activists paid runners 4,000–6,000 quanta per drone to disable the blockade units allowing aid access. Long-term, the flood opened new smuggling corridors through freshly submerged infrastructure that Bore Rats began mapping and runners began contracting through within the week.
